Yom Kippur in a bright synagogue: men in white kittels and boys in white shirts stand praying with deep feeling; soft white light streams in through the high windows and fills the room with a feeling of purity and cleanliness.

A parable scene: outside the gate of a clean, shining town of plain stone houses, servants carry sacks of rubbish out of the town and pile them far away; at the gate of a simple flat-roofed stone palace a kindly king with a golden crown watches, smiling with great joy because the town is clean.
On the eve of Yom Kippur, in a synagogue courtyard, one boy in a white shirt sincerely asks forgiveness from his friend; the friend smiles warmly and they shake hands, making up.

At sunset on a hill outside an ancient town of plain stone houses, an elderly judge of the Jewish court blows a long ram's-horn shofar; below on the road, freed servants walk happily home toward their green family fields carrying small bundles.
Yom Kippur eve: a father wearing a white kittel and his sons in clean white shirts walk together along a quiet stone street toward the synagogue, holding prayer books, calm and festive.

Yom Kippur in the synagogue: a man in a white kittel and tallit stands with his head bowed slightly, gently tapping his chest with his RIGHT fist while saying the confession from a prayer book with blank pages; the boy beside him does the same.

The end of Yom Kippur at nightfall: in the synagogue the holy ark stands open, the congregation in white kittels raise their faces with joy, and a man on the bimah blows a long shofar; through the window the first stars shine in the dark sky.

Right after Yom Kippur at night: at the dining table a father in a white kittel holds a silver cup for Havdalah and holds his fingers toward the flame of a candle in a tall glass jar that burned all day; his sons stand around watching, and the table is set with food ready to break the fast. No spice box.
On Yom Kippur a boy in a white shirt stands by a kitchen water tap holding an empty glass; he smiles and puts the glass down without drinking a single drop, choosing to fast.

On Yom Kippur a man with a cold lies in bed under a warm blanket, a tissue box beside him; he holds a prayer book with blank pages and prays quietly with moving lips; no food and no drink anywhere near him. Through the window a synagogue can be seen.

Inside a home on Yom Kippur, a seriously ill elderly man lies in bed; his grown son carefully helps him drink from a cup of water, while a kind doctor with a stethoscope and a kippa nods approvingly; through the window an ambulance waits outside.
A kind God-fearing doctor with a kippa and a stethoscope sits beside the bed of an elderly patient, listening carefully and seriously as the patient explains honestly how he feels.
On Yom Kippur at home, two small boys sit at a little table eating a simple meal of bread and soup; one of them has his eyes closed and his hand raised as he says a blessing before eating.
On Yom Kippur a boy who has a little mud on his fingers washes ONLY the muddy spot under a thin trickle of water at a sink, carefully keeping the rest of his hand dry.
Close-up in the morning: a boy's hands over a basin, pouring water from a two-handled washing cup over his fingers only up to the knuckles, not over the whole hand.
On Yom Kippur at the front door, a boy in a white shirt puts on soft cloth slippers, while his leather shoes stay neatly put away on the shoe rack.
Noon on Yom Kippur at home: a small boy eats a simple sandwich at the table, while his older brother in a white shirt sits nearby reading a prayer book, proud to be fasting.

Inside the ancient Holy Temple, the High Priest dressed in plain white linen garments stands before a huge heavy embroidered curtain, holding a golden pan with incense smoke rising, about to step behind the curtain. Plain white stone walls.

Night in a chamber of the Holy Temple lit by oil lamps: the High Priest sits learning Torah with elderly sages from open blank scrolls; a young priest standing beside him snaps his fingers to keep him awake; the stone floor is cold and bare.
In the white stone courtyard of the Holy Temple, two identical goats stand side by side, while the High Priest in white linen reaches into a small wooden box to draw two plain blank lots.
Late morning on the day before Passover in a stone courtyard: a boy feeds a few last pieces of bread to a goat, while his father looks up at the high sun to check the time.
A matzah bakery: on the table lie stalks of wheat, a bowl of flour and a pitcher of water; a baker quickly slides a thin round matzah into a glowing oven before the dough can rise.
A matzah bakery: men and boys knead the dough nonstop with busy hands, and on a shelf above them stands a large sand hourglass. No clock.
Close-up on a wooden board: a lump of dough with clear cracks across its surface; a baker boy points at the cracks with a surprised face.

In a kitchen before Passover, a boy puts a bowl of special pet food down for a happy dog and a cat, while his father carries the old bag of pet food out to be thrown away. All bags are plain with no labels.
Before Passover, a father and his sons carry bags of bread and crackers out of their plain stone house to remove all the chametz, smiling with energy.
A man closes a kitchen cupboard and seals its doors shut with strips of plain paper tape; he hides the key in a drawer.
A man stands on a stone pier by the sea, crumbling a leftover piece of bread and scattering the crumbs into the wind over the water; seagulls fly nearby.
section: עד מתי אוכלים ועד מתי מבטלים?

en: On the morning before Passover, a small fire burns chametz in a metal barrel in a yard; a father holds the feather, wooden spoon and paper bag from last night's search, and his sons watch from a safe distance.
At night a boy searches for chametz with a lit wax candle and a feather, holding a finger to his lips to stay silent, focused on his search.
At night a father searches inside the family car with a candle, looking between the seats, while his son empties the pockets of his school bag on the back seat.
At night a man searches a fenced balcony of a stone apartment building with a lit candle, checking the cracks and corners by the railing.
At night a boy kneels and searches under a bed by the light of a single wax candle; a flashlight lies on the floor beside him.
At night in a kitchen corner a father searches by candlelight and finds a small piece of bread about the size of an olive, without digging between the floor tiles.
A boy sits by a bookcase leafing through a book with blank pages, carefully checking whether any crumbs fell inside.
At night a boy searches a sparkling clean, shining room with a lit candle and a feather, checking anyway even though everything is spotless.

Before the search for chametz, a father hides small pieces of bread wrapped in little paper bags in easy places around the living room - on a shelf, a windowsill, behind a vase - while counting on his fingers.
In a grocery store before Passover, a father and son check a food package together and point to a small round plain stamp seal on the box. All packaging is blank with no writing.
A father opens a medicine cabinet: he sets a sweet syrup bottle aside on one shelf, and holds a small plain white pill to be swallowed. All bottles are blank with no labels.
A boy brushes his teeth at a bathroom sink, smiling into the mirror; the toothpaste tube is plain with no writing.

A kitchen counter with cleaning supplies, a dish soap bottle, a stack of paper cups, a roll of aluminum foil, baking paper and napkins; beside it a boy polishes a shoe with shoe polish. All items are plain with no labels.
Evening: a man fills clay jugs with water from a stone well, and sets them in a cool, dark stone cellar to rest overnight.
In a matzah bakery, a baker with a long wooden paddle slides thin round matzot into a blazing hot brick oven with roaring fire inside.
At a matzah bakery counter, a man hands money to the baker right away while receiving a stack of round hand-made matzot wrapped in plain paper; both smile. Coins and bills have no numbers.
Afternoon before Passover at home: a father irons a white shirt and a boy polishes his shoes, while a pot cooks on the stove; a sewing machine in the corner stays covered.
section: מה אסור ומה מתר אחר חצות?

en: Morning before Passover at a synagogue entrance: a father holds the hand of his small firstborn son as they walk in together.
Morning before Passover in a study hall: a man finishes the last page of a big volume with blank pages, and the men around the table rejoice and share plates of cake and cups of juice.
On a white tablecloth lie the four species: one yellow etrog, one tall lulav palm branch, three myrtle branches and two willow branches; a boy looks at them with wonder.
A man holds up a tall, straight lulav with tightly closed green leaves and examines it carefully; on the table beside him lies a bent, crooked lulav for comparison.
Close-up: a boy holds a magnifying glass over a myrtle branch whose leaves grow in neat rings of three at the same height, like a braid.
A boy compares two branches side by side on a table: one willow branch with long, narrow, smooth-edged leaves and a reddish stem, and one branch with saw-toothed leaves and a green stem.
At a market stall of etrogs, a father and son admire a beautiful yellow etrog in their hands, while on the stall a perfectly round ball-shaped citron and a dark one lie set aside.
Morning in a synagogue during Sukkot: sunlight streams through the windows as men in tallitot and boys hold their four species during the morning prayers.
A man holds the lulav bundle in his RIGHT hand and the etrog in his LEFT hand, pressing them together, the lulav's spine facing him and the etrog's stem pointing down.
A boy in a synagogue waves his lulav and etrog forward, arms stretched out and drawing back toward his chest, with small motion lines showing the waving.
During Hallel in the synagogue, a father helps his small son hold his own little lulav and etrog, guiding his hands to wave them.
In a synagogue during Sukkot, men and boys holding their four species walk in a circle around the bimah, where a man holds a Torah scroll in its cover; the holy ark stands open.
On Hoshana Rabba in a synagogue, a man beats a bundle of five willow branches on the floor, and small green leaves scatter around his feet.
After Sukkot, a boy respectfully places his lulav and willow branches on a neat pile of trimmed garden branches in the corner of the yard, not in a garbage can.
Late afternoon on the last day of Sukkot, a boy gently kisses the doorpost of the decorated sukkah as he says goodbye, while his father sits inside at the table.
Before the holiday, a man stands on a ladder removing a square section of the leafy branches from the roof of his sukkah, leaving an open gap to the sky.
Shemini Atzeret night: a family table set inside the house with festive dishes and candles; the father makes kiddush over a silver cup; through the window an empty sukkah stands outside in the yard.
A man stands praying in a synagogue, and through the window rain clouds gather and the first drops of rain begin to fall.
On Simchat Torah, many small boys gather at the bimah under a large tallit spread over them like a canopy, together with an older man, all happy, beside an open Torah scroll.
On Simchat Torah, two honored men stand at the bimah under a tallit canopy, each beside an open Torah scroll, one at its end and one at its beginning, while the congregation cheers.
On Simchat Torah, men dance in a circle holding Torah scrolls in their covers, clapping and singing joyfully; boys ride on their fathers' shoulders.
A father and his son stand in front of the ancient stone Western Wall, the father's hand on his son's shoulder, both quietly remembering the destruction, with sorrowful but hopeful faces.
Ancient Jerusalem with high stone walls, surrounded by the tents and campfires of the Babylonian army laying siege; the city gates are shut. No fighting, no blood.
Ezra the scribe, an old man with a white beard, stands on a wooden platform in Jerusalem holding an open Torah scroll with blank parchment, reading to a large crowd of men listening with attention.
Roman soldiers break through a section of the high stone wall of ancient Jerusalem; stones tumble down from the breach and dust rises. No blood, no fighting between people.
Evening of a fast day: a boy leans out of a window and points at three stars appearing in the darkening sky, while his father in the background prepares a meal to break the fast.
A boy who has just taken one bite of an apple suddenly remembers it is a fast day; he stops, puts his hand on his forehead in surprise and sets the apple down.
A man with the flu lies in bed under a blanket with a thermometer in his mouth; beside him on a tray is a simple bowl of soup and a glass of water.
On a fast day at home, two small boys eat simple bread and cheese at the table, while their father sits nearby reading a book with blank pages.
On Tisha B'Av, a boy with a little mud on his knee wipes ONLY the muddy spot with a wet cloth, while a full bathtub nearby stays unused.
On Tisha B'Av, at the entrance to a synagogue, men and boys wear simple cloth slippers; leather shoes are not worn by anyone.
On Tisha B'Av, a man sits on the floor reading quietly from a book with blank pages, with a sad and thoughtful face; his son sits on the floor beside him.
On Tisha B'Av, a man at a doorway hands a basket of food for after the fast to a poor man, with a serious, gentle face and no cheerful greeting.
Night of Tisha B'Av in a dim synagogue lit only by a few small candles: men sit on the floor and on low stools, and the reader recites from a blank scroll in a sad voice.
Tisha B'Av morning in a synagogue: the holy ark stands with its decorative curtain removed, showing plain wooden doors; men pray without tallit and without tefillin.
Tisha B'Av at home: small boys in cloth slippers sit at the table eating plain bread, while an older boy sits on the floor reading quietly.
